meta.title: Who really said "For most of history, Anonymous was a woman"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Woolf's words. The line paraphrases A Room of One's Own (1929): "I would venture to guess that Anon... was often a woman."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'For most of history, Anonymous was a woman'?
meta.ogDescription: A paraphrase, not a quotation. Woolf actually wrote that Anon, "who wrote so many poems without signing them, was often a woman" (1929).

answer.label: Not Virginia Woolf’s words — a modern paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: The thought is Woolf’s, but the snappy wording is not. In A Room of One’s Own (1929), chapter 3, she wrote: “I would venture to guess that Anon, who wrote so many poems without signing them, was often a woman.” “For most of history, Anonymous was a woman” is a later paraphrase found nowhere in her text.

source.heading: What Woolf actually wrote
source.excerpt: When, however, one reads of a witch being ducked, of a woman possessed by devils, of a wise woman selling herbs, or even of a very remarkable man who had a mother, then I think we are on the track of a lost novelist, a suppressed poet, of some mute and inglorious Jane Austen, some Emily Brontë who dashed her brains out on the moor or mopped and mowed about the highways crazed with the torture that her gift had put her to. Indeed, I would venture to guess that Anon, who wrote so many poems without signing them, was often a woman. It was a woman Edward Fitzgerald, I think, suggested who made the ballads and the folk-songs, crooning them to her children, beguiling her spinning with them, or the length of the winter’s night.
trail: Primary text. The Hogarth Press edition of A Room of One’s Own held by the Internet Archive contains the sentence “Indeed, I would venture to guess that Anon, who wrote so many poems without signing them, was often a woman” in chapter 3 (Internet Archive ↗).

Wikiquote. Woolf’s Wikiquote page lists the genuine sentence under A Room of One’s Own (Ch. 3) with the note that it is “very often misquoted as ‘For most of history, Anonymous was a woman’” (Wikiquote ↗).
Woolf specialists. The Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain’s misquotations page calls the popular line a paraphrase of the chapter-3 sentence, reworded to make it snappier (VWSGB ↗).
Quote Investigator. A search of quoteinvestigator.com found no article on this line, so Wikiquote and the Woolf Society serve as the specialist anchors here.
source.excerptNote: Text checked against the Hogarth Press “new edition” of 1935 on the Internet Archive, which reproduces the 1929 text. The popular line “For most of history, Anonymous was a woman” appears nowhere in the essay. Note that at least one free online transcription misprints “signing” as “singing.”

source.rightsNote: Woolf’s genuine sentence comes from A Room of One’s Own, first published in 1929, before the 1931 cutoff, so that text is in the public domain in the United States. The short “For most of history” paraphrase has no identified author or first publication, so we assert no separate rights status for that wording.

author.name: Virginia Woolf
author.heading: About Virginia Woolf
author.bio: Virginia Woolf was an English modernist novelist and essayist, author of Mrs Dalloway and To the Lighthouse, and a pioneer of stream-of-consciousness narration. A Room of One’s Own (1929) grew out of two papers she read to women students at Newnham and Girton colleges, Cambridge, in October 1928. It became one of the founding texts of feminist literary criticism, and the “Anon” sentence comes from its third chapter.

misattribution.heading: How the paraphrase took over
misattribution.intro: The short wording is Woolf’s idea, condensed by others. Over time the condensed form has come to be presented as her own words, inside quotation marks.

items.who: “For most of history, Anonymous was a woman.” — Virginia Woolf
items.why: The shortened line circulates as a direct Woolf quotation, often with no source. For example, a Goodreads author blog post of 4 January 2012 is headed with it and credits Woolf without citing any book or page (Goodreads ↗). Wikiquote calls it “very often misquoted” (Wikiquote ↗).

The phrase also works as a title that nods to Woolf. The Anonymous Was A Woman grant for women artists, begun in 1996, says its name “refers to a line in Virginia Woolf’s A Room of One’s Own” (Anonymous Was A Woman ↗). Quotations scholar Fred Shapiro used the same title for a 2011 Yale Alumni Magazine essay, and in it he quotes Woolf’s exact sentence (Yale Alumni Magazine ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Woolf wrote: “I would venture to guess that Anon, who wrote so many poems without signing them, was often a woman” (A Room of One’s Own, 1929, ch. 3). The Woolf Society classes the popular version as a paraphrase (VWSGB ↗).

context.heading: Why the sentence mattered
lead: The line comes from the chapter where Woolf imagines “Shakespeare’s sister,” a woman of equal genius whom law, custom and poverty keep from ever writing. Woolf reads traces of buried talent in the record: the witch ducked, the wise woman selling herbs. Her guess about “Anon” extends that argument to the unsigned ballads and folk-songs of the past.

Her wording is deliberately tentative: “I would venture to guess,” and “often,” not “always.” The popular paraphrase drops both hedges and adds “for most of history.” That makes it a sweeping historical claim, which Woolf herself did not put in those words.
detailsBody: A Room of One’s Own grew from two papers Woolf read to the Newnham Arts Society and the ODTAA Society at Girton College, Cambridge, in October 1928. It was published in 1929 by the Hogarth Press in Britain and Harcourt Brace in the United States (Wikipedia ↗).
